questions.q: What are the three states every Azure Quantum job moves through?
options: Draft, Review, Published
Waiting, Executing, Succeeded/Failed
Created, Deleted, Archived
Local, Cloud, Hybrid
questions.explain: Every submitted job -- regardless of target -- moves through Waiting (queued), Executing (running), and finally Succeeded or Failed.

questions.q: Why is submitting a job to Azure Quantum not synchronous the way calling a local simulator function is?
options: You get a job handle back immediately, and the actual computation runs elsewhere on its own schedule -- your code either polls status in a loop or uses a helper that polls internally
Azure Quantum jobs always complete instantly with no delay
Submission always fails on the first attempt by design
Jobs run entirely inside the submitting script's own process
questions.explain: Submission returns a job handle/ID right away; the job itself executes asynchronously, requiring polling (manual via job show, or via job.wait_until_completed() in the SDK) to learn when it's done.

questions.q: What does `job.wait_until_completed()` do in the azure-quantum Python SDK, as described in the lesson?
options: It cancels the job immediately
It blocks the script, internally polling the job's status until it finishes
It submits a brand new job with the same parameters
It converts the job's target from hardware to simulator
questions.explain: wait_until_completed() does exactly the polling loop you'd otherwise write by hand with repeated status checks, blocking until the job reaches a terminal state.

questions.q: How does the result payload differ between a simulator/real-hardware job and a resource-estimator job?
options: They are always identical in format
Simulator/hardware jobs return a histogram of measured bitstrings; resource-estimator jobs return a structured hardware-requirements report (physical qubits, runtime), not measurement outcomes
Resource-estimator jobs always return an error
Simulator jobs never return any results at all
questions.explain: Simulator and hardware jobs produce a measurement histogram; the resource estimator's 'result' is a hardware-requirements projection, a fundamentally different payload shape that code must handle differently.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend dry-running a program on a simulator before submitting it to a real-hardware target?
options: Real hardware jobs can queue behind other customers' jobs and accrue real cost per job/shot, so validating correctness cheaply and quickly on a simulator first avoids paying for and waiting on a job that was going to fail anyway
Simulators are required by Azure Quantum's terms of service before any hardware job
Real hardware targets do not accept Q# programs at all
There is no practical reason -- it's purely a stylistic preference
questions.explain: Real hardware shares a physical device across customers (queueing) and accrues cost per job/shot; debugging on a free, fast, exact simulator first avoids wasting both time and money on a job that fails due to a logic bug.
